clue.text: Attend opening of two presents to carry out tattoo

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its very start, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: to attend is to BE AT an event
first letter of two
two senses of present: HERE (in attendance) and TREAT (a gift)

explanation.surface: Someone opens two presents and then, oddly, has to go off and get a tattoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tattoo' is not body ink but the military evening display; BEAT THE RETREAT is the drum ceremony performed at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: Beating the retreat is the military ceremony of drums at dusk, which is what a tattoo display is, so it means performing one.

clue.text: Going over correspondence, not hear gongs

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to leave out the word that follows from the longer word
going over suggests turning something over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: symmetry is exact correspondence between two halves
a judge will hear, or try, a case

explanation.surface: Someone goes through their post without listening, and gongs are involved somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' is the judge's sense, to hear a case, and those letters come out before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Gongs is slang for awards or medals, and Emmys are the American television industry's awards.

clue.text: Turning left chap's checked what's happening

indicators.note: turning round makes a word run the opposite way
the chap is checked, held in, by the surrounding letters

blocks.note: left, as in departed
a chap is a he

explanation.surface: A man turning left gets stopped and asked what's going on.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of chap's is 'is': the chap is held inside the turned-round word.
explanation.definitionFit: The new is the latest thing, the current trend, so it is what is happening now.

clue.text: Bond's third replacement infiltrates Chinese Empire State concert

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the Han are China's main ethnic group
Bond is agent 007; write the zeros as OO and replace the third character, the 7, with TEN
New York is the Empire State

explanation.surface: A spy's stand-in sneaks into a Chinese performance at New York's Empire State Building.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empire State is New York's nickname; 007's number is played with by putting TEN in place of its last digit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hootenanny is an informal folk-music gathering or party, an American kind of concert.

clue.text: This knot's a little more effective

indicators.note: only a little of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: spans the end of more and the start of effective

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a particular knot as slightly better than the alternatives.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef knot is the square knot used by sailors to tie reefing lines, a standard knot type.

clue.text: Ten-second change in wind at most these days

indicators.note: the Roman ten and the abbreviation for second are told to change places

blocks.note: to wind is to twist
max, short for maximum, means at most

explanation.surface: A time-trial result changes by a tenth of a second depending on the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: In TWIST MAX the X (ten) and the S (second) swap places. The puzzle appeared on 27 December, so 'these days' is the period it was published in.
explanation.definitionFit: Twixtmas is the informal name for the days between Christmas and New Year, when this puzzle ran.

clue.text: Unlikely to be rushed off on a picnic?

blocks.note: first meaning: relaxed, never hurried off one's feet
second meaning: playing on 'no picnic' for something hard, being on one means the going is easy

explanation.walkthrough: 'No picnic' means difficult, so being on a picnic is the opposite: the going is easy. The question mark flags that playful sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Easygoing describes a relaxed temperament, someone hard to hurry, and punningly the easy going of a picnic outing.

clue.text: Anybody's guess why Christmas cracker disappoints?

blocks.note: first meaning: nobody can predict it
second meaning: a cracker with no motto or joke inside is a letdown

explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is the paper tube pulled apart at British Christmas dinners, containing a hat, a trinket and a printed motto or joke; the second reading takes the phrase literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means it is impossible to predict, which is what calling something anybody's guess conveys.

clue.text: Too bedraggled to be hating rain

indicators.note: something bedraggled is messed up and untidy, so the letters are put in disorder

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone soaked through by the weather is too miserable to enjoy rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' looks like link words but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Into the bargain is an idiom meaning as well or in addition, the same sense as 'too'.

clue.text: Nothing orbiting earth star

indicators.note: to orbit is to go round, so one word encircles the other

blocks.note: none is nothing
umber is a brown earth used as a pigment

explanation.surface: An astronomy fact: nothing goes round the earth like a star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earth' and 'star' set an astronomical scene, but earth is a painter's pigment and the star is a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: A number one is the top performer or chart-topping act, a leading celebrity, which a star is.

clue.text: Turn out problem children

blocks.note: first meaning: to come out, result or emerge
second meaning: a matter of concern
third meaning: offspring

explanation.walkthrough: This is a triple definition: 'children' is a third meaning, the legal word for offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers emerging as a result, a point of concern, and a person's offspring in legal language.

clue.text: Expletive-laden part of play filmed on location?

blocks.note: OB is an outside broadcast, filmed away from the studio
a scene is a section of a play

explanation.surface: A sweary bit of a play is shot on location rather than on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: OB is the abbreviation for outside broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Language full of expletives is foul and offensive, and obscene means just that kind of indecent swearing.

clue.text: Suggestion for contrivance that filters out gun's smoke in Western?

indicators.note: filtering something out removes it, so letters are taken away
a contrivance is something made up and rearranged, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A film-maker asks for a device to stop gun smoke spoiling a cowboy movie scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing G, U, N, S from SUGGESTION leaves GESTIO for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A stogie is a long, cheap cigar, named after Conestoga wagon drivers of the American West, so a smoke in a Western.

clue.text: High knees, maybe, in cycling club?

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round in a loop, the last coming to the front

blocks.note: a high is a drug trip
knees are an example of joints

explanation.surface: A cycling club where riders are drilled to raise their knees high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High knees' looks like an exercise; the S at the end of TRIPJOINTS cycles to the front. A club here is a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip joint is a nightclub featuring striptease, so club is a broad hypernym for it.

clue.text: In consultation cover who appears in doctor's absence?

indicators.note: a consultation is a spoken exchange, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: to cover something is to hide it

explanation.surface: A locum covers for a doctor who is away from the surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Hyde is the evil alter ego who appears when Dr Jekyll is absent in Stevenson's story.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's novella Hyde emerges whenever Dr Jekyll's own personality is gone, so he shows up when the doctor is away.

clue.text: Hose-wearer presumably also had this pair in hand

definitions.note: a clause rather than a noun, fair because the answer splits as DOUBLET ON, which says what the man in hose was also wearing

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: a man in hose would have had his jacket-like top garment on too
second meaning: in bridge, a holding of exactly two cards in a suit

explanation.walkthrough: In Tudor times hose (tights) were worn with a doublet, a close-fitting jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games a doubleton is a holding of only two cards in one suit, so a pair within a dealt hand.

clue.text: The actors will receive no more than this gelding

blocks.note: the actors in a production are the cast

blocks.clueFragment: will receive no more than this
blocks.note: a ration is the fixed allowance, all one gets

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted producer tells the company how little they will be paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gelding' is not the horse here but the operation that produces one.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelding is the act of neutering a male animal, which is the operation called castration.

clue.text: During after-work beer I made one enemy

indicators.note: being made into something else means one item is swapped for another

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
a pint is a glass of beer
taken as written, replacing I

explanation.surface: Over an after-work drink someone fell out with a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the beer behind the work; 'During' sets the swap inside the beer, where the Roman-looking I becomes the word one.
explanation.definitionFit: An opponent is someone you contend against, an adversary or enemy.

clue.text: Censor seen publicly stripped, then flogged

indicators.note: stripping peels off the outer layer, so the outside letters go
something flogged is beaten about, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the phrase without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tabloid tale: a censor caught naked in public and then whipped.
explanation.definitionFit: To blue-pencil is to cut or censor text, from the editor's blue pencil used for deletions.

clue.text: Source of great amusement, shaggy dog story about senior army staff

definitions.note: defines A GAS, read as two words

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a shaggy dog story is a long, rambling tale

explanation.surface: A long rambling joke about army brass proves hugely entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions plus wordplay: read as A GAS it is something hilarious; as one word it is the plural of aga, an Ottoman commander.
explanation.definitionFit: An aga was a high-ranking Turkish military officer, so agas are senior army commanders; a gas is slang for great fun.

clue.text: Surrounded by Scots initially, not wanting to beg

indicators.note: not wanting something means doing without it, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: initially means at first, to begin with
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beggar among Scotsmen at first refuses to ask for money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots' marks the definition as a Scottish word. TO BEGIN WITH loses TO BEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Inwith is a Scots preposition meaning within or inside, so enclosed or surrounded by something.

clue.text: Duke of Normandy knight administered with balls

blocks.note: Rollo was the Viking founder of the duchy of Normandy
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A medieval duke dubs a knight with ceremonial orb in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'balls' are the rolling ball of a deodorant applicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll-on product, typically deodorant, is applied by a rotating ball in its tip.

clue.text: The first dozen talking about case that contains separate articles

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so the articles go within

blocks.note: a jury of twelve discusses a case
AN and A, the indefinite articles, inserted at different points

explanation.surface: Twelve jurors deliberate over a case involving several newspaper pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separate' means AN and A go into different gaps. 'The first' is the first of a dozen months.
explanation.definitionFit: January is the opening month of the year, so it is the first of the calendar's twelve.

clue.text: Set to be assigned a new nurse

blocks.note: taken as written
N is short for new
to set, as a jelly does, is to gel

explanation.surface: A ward is all set for a new nurse to be allocated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' leads the clue but its piece goes last, after A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurses are affectionately called angels for their caring work, as in 'angel of mercy'.

clue.text: Spotted trouble, picking up cab in Bow

indicators.note: picking up a sound means hearing it, so the word goes by ear

blocks.note: a hackney cab, as said by a Cockney who drops the H

explanation.surface: A London cabbie in the East End spots trouble ahead and picks up a fare.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is in London's East End, so 'in Bow' means Cockney speech with its dropped H; a hackney carriage is the formal name for a taxi.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is a skin condition producing spots, so it is literally trouble with spots.

clue.text: Not in favour of gossip columns

indicators.note: gossip is spoken chatter, so we go by the word's sound

blocks.note: anti means opposed

explanation.surface: Someone disapproves of the newspaper gossip pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Columns' looks like newspaper columns; it is architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: Antae are square pilasters at the ends of a temple's side walls, a type of architectural pillar.

clue.text: Caught guy with trap offering his twopenceworth?

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a guy is a him
in, as in 'in company with'
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: A poacher caught with a trap has something to say for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Twopenceworth (two pennies' worth) is a British phrase for an unasked-for opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiming in means interrupting with an opinion, which is adding one's two pennies' worth to a conversation.

clue.text: Challengers through one round, the venue for the next?

definitions.text: Challengers through one round, the venue for the next?

blocks.note: surface reading: competitors who have survived a round of a knockout tournament
setter's reading: golfers who have finished their round of eighteen holes head to the clubhouse bar for another round, of drinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' means a round of golf, then a round of drinks; the clubhouse bar is the place golfers go after the eighteenth hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers call the clubhouse bar by this jocular name because it follows the last hole of a full course.
